19652-a-ball-player-s-career-being-the-p:
Marshalltown, Iowa, opens this baseball memoir, praised as a handsome town of some thirteen thousand people. A Ball Player's Career presents itself as the personal experiences and recollections of its player-author. Books of this kind came from the first stars of professional baseball. They let fans hear the game described by a man who played it.

Readers get the early pro game from inside: travel, pay, crowds, and clubhouse life. Such memoirs helped turn ballplayers into national figures. They also fixed stories that later histories would test. The value here is the first-hand voice from baseball's rough early decades. Few records of that era feel this direct.
19734-the-fairy-book-the-best-popular-st:
The Fairy Book promises the best popular fairy stories, selected and rendered anew. Its preface speaks plainly to parents and children. In real life, it warns, beautiful people are not always good. Ugly people are not always wicked either. Elder sisters are not all ungenerous, nor stepmothers all cruel. Tender young hearts, it says, are reached by fancy as soon as by reason.

Retellings shaped how generations first met fairy tales. Editors softened some cruelties and kept the wonders. A preface like this one argues for the tales' honesty. It defends fancy as a teacher in its own right. The stories inside are the shared stock of childhood. This book shows Victorians handing that stock down, carefully.
19908-essays-on-scandinavian-literature:
Hjalmar Hjorth Boyesen published Essays on Scandinavian Literature in 1895. His Henrik Ibsen chapter, he explains, grew into its own book. That three-hundred-page study appeared the year before. It must be read as supplementary to this volume. His Björnson chapter nearly suffered the same expansion. Only heroic condensation kept it inside these covers. Boyesen, a Norwegian immigrant, interpreted the North for America.

Boyesen taught literature at Columbia and wrote novels too. He knew Ibsen's Norway from inside its culture. These essays carry Scandinavian writing to English readers early. Ibsen, Björnson, and their peers get full, serious treatment. The book marks America's discovery of modern Northern letters. Its enthusiasm still instructs and persuades.
19914-arabic-authors-a-manual-of-arabian:
Arabic Authors is a manual of Arabian history and literature by F. F. Arbuthnot. It hopes for a day when Oriental languages fill leisure hours. So much is to be learnt from Oriental literature, the author argues. King's College, London, is praised as full of promise for such study. A future generation thirsting for knowledge might study Arabic as a pastime. The manual itself opens that door for English readers.

Arbuthnot translated and promoted Eastern literature in Victorian Britain. His manual surveys poets, historians, and storytellers of Arabia. Short lives and work-lists guide beginners through centuries. The Thousand and One Nights looms over such surveys. This one stays practical, a handbook rather than a romance. It shows Oriental studies entering general culture.
19998-rural-architecture:
Lewis F. Allen wrote Rural Architecture to improve American farm buildings. Friends solicited the book, Allen says, believing he could help landholders. Without their urging, these pages would probably never have appeared. Practical farmers are his declared audience throughout. Plans for farmhouses, barns, and outbuildings fill the volume. Allen was a noted New York stock breeder and agricultural editor.

Farm architecture was a reform cause in the 1850s. Bad barns wasted stock, feed, and labor visibly. Allen gives designs, costs, and siting advice in full. His own farming success backed the authority claimed. The book belongs with Downing's country-house movement. It shows the model farm becoming an American ideal.
20101-under-fire:
Under Fire is a tale of soldiers, home, and the pride of a plains family. A soldier son comes home with an honored name in his trade. His parents glow with pride to have him under their roof again. Two sturdy, plains-bred little Cranstons add noise and joy to the house.

War still hangs over such a homecoming in the tale. Health, fame, and family love meet the strain of service life. The book shows how frontier homes bore the costs of war. Readers get a warm, tense story of return after danger and long absence.
20131-the-mask-a-story-of-love-and-adven:
Arthur Hornblow published The Mask in 1913, a story of love and adventure. News breaks of a huge gem found after blasting at some rocks. The land sits next to tracts of the Americo-African Mining Company. Some say the firm is already buying the ground for itself.

If true, the giant stone means a windfall for its Yankee owners. Diamonds, deals, and desire drive a tale set around African mines. The mask of the title hints at hidden faces and false shows. Readers get romance and risk in the world of gems and gold.
20406-epic-and-romance-essays-on-medieva:
W. P. Ker, a leading scholar of old literature, wrote Epic and Romance to explain the great stories of medieval Europe. The essays treat heroic poems, sagas, and romances as serious art. Ker writes for readers who want the old tales understood, not merely retold.

One essay wrestles with the Icelandic historian Sturla and the rivalry of a king and his father-in-law, Duke Skule. Ker praises the work of his friend Dr. Björn Magnússon Olsen on these hard problems. The book remains a guide to how epic strength and romance wonder grew side by side.
20572-marie-claire:
Marie-Claire is Marguerite Audoux's novel of a French orphan girl, drawn from the writer's own hard childhood. Marie-Claire grows up in a convent orphanage and goes out to work on farms and in service. The telling is plain, close, and quietly heartbreaking.

She remembers her sister's torments in their childhood games. The girl used to collect earthworms and hold them up close to her face. When she claimed she was no longer in pain, their keeper sent them both outdoors. One day her sister threw a handful of earthworms onto her dress. Such small cruelties mark the book's truthful eye.
20631-chosen-peoples-being-the-first-art:
Chosen Peoples, published in 1919, was the first Arthur Davis Memorial Lecture, delivered by Israel Zangwill. Zangwill, the Anglo-Jewish novelist, took up the hard idea of the chosen people. He spoke just after a war that had shown where racial pride could lead.

The recent show of racial arrogance in Germany, he notes, has handed the Allies a new weapon. An American writer in the Bookman declared that Germanism is Judaism. The proposition, Zangwill warns, contains just that dash of truth which is more dangerous than a falsehood. The lecture untangles that dash with care.
20657-tales-from-shakespeare:
Charles and Mary Lamb wrote Tales from Shakespeare to retell the plays as stories for young readers. Charles took the tragedies and Mary the comedies, in retellings first published in 1807. Their versions brought Shakespeare into the nursery without flattening his plots.

The Tempest opens the book. There was once an old man whose name was Prospero, and his daughter Miranda, a very beautiful young lady. She came to the island so young that she had no memory of any human face but her father's. The Lambs' plain, warm style has carried readers into Shakespeare for two centuries.
20702-a-general-plan-for-a-mail-communic:
A General Plan for a Mail Communication by Steam proposes regular steam packet routes to carry Britain's mail overseas. When sails ruled, letters waited on wind and season. The plan argues that steam can give the mail fixed days and faster passages between Great Britain and its distant ports.

It leans on expert proof. Mr. Napier of Glasgow, called an able and practical engineer, told the Post Office Commissioners in 1836 what steamers could do. Boats of 240 horsepower and 620 tons, he said, could be furnished at known prices. Such pamphlets helped push Britain into the steam age of world mail.
20733-critical-miscellanies-vol-1-of-3-e:
Robespierre and the close of the Reign of Terror open the first essay in Critical Miscellanies. The writer takes up a new French book on the fall of Robespierre. Those events bear the calendar name of Thermidor, in Year Two of the French Republic.

Victorian essay craft is on full show here, with long views of men and ideas. The piece weighs how a revolution turned on its own leaders. Later essays in the set treat other great figures and books. Readers who like bold, old-style literary essays will find strong opinions, wide reading, and prose built for argument rather than speed.
20740-myths-and-legends-of-all-nations-f:
Prometheus and Epimetheus, Forethought and Afterthought, open Myths and Legends of All Nations. The two brothers were sons of Titans who fought Jupiter and were chained below. Yet the brothers, for some reason, escaped that harsh fate.

Famed tales from Greece and other lands fill the book, retold in clear prose for general readers. Gods, heroes, gifts of fire, and hard lessons follow one after another. Such sets once served as a first door into world myth for many homes. The simple retelling keeps the old plots clear while trimming the hard parts of the source tales.
20784-eighth-annual-report-of-the-bureau:
Pueblo building in Tusayan and Cibola leads the eighth annual report of the Bureau of Ethnology. Victor Mindeleff studied those towns of stone and adobe in close detail. James Stevenson adds a study of a Navajo rite and its mythic sand painting.

Staff work by Cosmos Mindeleff, Garrick Mallery, James Mooney, and Jeremiah Curtin fills the report. The bureau sent trained men to record native life before it changed. Their plates and plans keep much that would else be lost. This 1886-87 volume is a rich trove for students of the native Southwest and its old towns.
20902-the-clyde-mystery-a-study-in-forge:
Plates from Gillen, learned boards, and Scots societies crowd the thanks in The Clyde Mystery. Andrew Lang turns to finds claimed as relics near the Clyde. Forgery and folklore, his subtitle warns, both haunt the case at hand.

Lang, a famed folklorist, tests stones and tales said to prove old Scots glory. He weighs proof with wit, lore, and a sceptic's sharp eye. The Clyde finds had stirred pride and doubt in learned Scotland. His study shows how scholars sort true relics from fond fakes, a craft as gripping as the finds themselves when told by Lang.
20953-by-the-christmas-fire:
Turning a sword to a pruning hook takes a smith, but a bayonet to a poker takes none. Samuel McChord Crothers opens By the Christmas Fire, from 1908, on that fireside thought. Severed from its rifle, the blade's new work is to coax winter flames.

Crothers, a beloved essayist and preacher, gathers warm talks for the Christmas season. Home, giving, faith, and good humour glow through his gentle pages. His essays were famed for kindness lit by quiet wit. This book suits slow winter reading, each piece a small fire of its own against the cold and dark outside.
21053-an-anthology-of-german-literature:
Sixty-nine lines of alliterative verse are all that survive of Germany's oldest heroic song, Calvin Thomas notes. The Kassel manuscript of the eighth or ninth century keeps that fragment safe. Its tongue mixes Low and High German, with gaps and doubtful words.

Thomas's anthology of German literature spans that fragment to near his own day of 1906. Poems, plays, tales, and essays appear in English versions with learned notes. He built the book for American students new to German letters. It maps a vast literature in one volume, from heroic lays to Goethe and beyond, with a teacher's steady hand.
21090-brief-history-of-english-and-ameri:
Henry A. Beers combined his outline sketches of English and American literature into this single brief history. It was published in New York, with copyrights running from 1886 to 1897. John Fletcher Hurst added an introduction and extra chapters on religious and theological writing in both countries. The book was aimed at students and general readers.

Beers moves through the main writers and periods of two literatures in a compact survey. Hurst argues that preachers and students of religion alike need real knowledge of literature. Indexes and page markers help readers use it as a reference. It shows how the two literatures were taught side by side in its day.
21098-the-independence-of-claire:
Claire Gifford has lived for three years in a Brussels pension when Mrs George de Horne Vaizey's novel opens. She stands in the salon asking herself one question: can she marry the man proposed for her? Her brain says she must, out of duty to her family, while her heart rebels.

Vaizey writes about young, well-brought-up women of Edwardian times, their money worries, clothes, parties, and marriage choices. Claire seems headed for a big mistake before matters sort themselves out. The title points to her real struggle, which is less about one suitor than about standing on her own feet and choosing her own life.
21214-the-law-and-lawyers-of-pickwick-a-:
Frank Lockwood, a Queen's Counsel and Member of Parliament, delivered this lecture in York and then in London in December 1893. Its subject is the law and lawyers of Dickens's Pickwick Papers. Lord Russell of Killowen, then Attorney General, introduced him at Morley Hall in Hackney. The Roxburghe Press printed the lecture in 1894.

Lockwood, himself a witty advocate, examines Sergeant Buzfuz and the famous trial of Bardell against Pickwick. That breach of promise case turns on chops, tomata sauce, and comic cross talk. He explains the real law behind Dickens's fun. An original drawing of Buzfuz fronts the little book.
21303-devon-boys-a-tale-of-the-north-sho:
Three boarders at Barnstaple Grammar School spend their summer holiday on Devon's north shore in George Manville Fenn's tale, set in 1752. Bob Chowne is a doctor's cross-grained son, and Bigley Uggleston is a fisherman's pleasant boy. Sep Duncan, the narrator, is a naval officer's son whose father has just bought a stretch of cliffs.

The boys blast a rock from the cliff top and uncover a rich vein of galena, lead and silver ore. Sep's father opens a mine on the spot. Escapades follow: rescues at sea by a French smuggler and a French attack aimed at twenty boxes of silver bullion stored from the mine.
21390-the-golden-grasshopper-a-story-of-:
Ernst Verner, a Dutch boy, tells his own tale in W. H. G. Kingston's The Golden Grasshopper. His parents died in Holland for their Protestant faith, and he reaches an England split by creed. Between King Edward, Queen Mary, and Queen Elizabeth, belief could cost a life.

The story first came out in 1870 as The Royal Merchant, in the days of Sir Thomas Gresham. Gresham, the great London merchant, stands at the heart of the tale's world of trade. Boys on the run, a hostile priest, and slow Channel crossings add the peril. Kingston revised the book near the end of his life.
21404-from-powder-monkey-to-admiral-a-st:
Three boys join the navy at its lowest rung in W. H. G. Kingston's From Powder Monkey to Admiral. Kingston wrote the story for the Boys' Own Paper when that paper first started. His aim was to show how a plain lad might climb to the top rank.

Powder monkeys ran powder to the guns in battle, small targets who often lived through fights. Real men like Benbow and Hopson had made just that climb before. The three boys share the usual run of Kingston sea adventures. Only one of them, though, wins his way to the quarterdeck and a midshipman's place.
21724-the-handbook-of-soap-manufacture:
Two chemists, W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, wrote this practical handbook of soap making, published in London in 1908. The opening chapter defines soap and explains how it cleans, through the splitting of fats by water and alkali. Later chapters take up the make-up of oils and fats and how they turn into soap.

The authors cover old research, modern methods, and the tools and tests a working soap maker needs. Twenty-seven pictures help show plant and process. The book was made for the trade, not the home kitchen. It gives a clear snapshot of factory soap making at the start of the twentieth century, chemistry and craft side by side.
21908-chums-of-the-camp-fire:
Bullfrog hunting opens Chums of the Camp Fire, a 1915 boys' book by Lawrence J. Leslie. Steve, Toby, and Max count thirteen frog saddles and aim for twenty before they quit. Toby stammers his tallies while the boys dream of the Dismal Swamp, where a bushel basket might be filled. The chapters roll into the woods: a terrible roar, a mysterious ham thrower, and a wild animal trap.

A strange disappearance and a plot against the missing link raise the stakes before the last camp fire. Leslie writes in the brisk series style, each chapter a small adventure with a hook. The frontispiece shows Max sure they can capture the monkey. It is cheerful outdoor fiction for boys of the camping age, all appetite and schemes.
21957-the-psychology-of-singing-a-ration:
Singing teachers are put on trial in David C. Taylor's The Psychology of Singing, first published in 1908 and reprinted in 1922. Taylor calls his book a rational method of voice culture built on a study of all systems, ancient and modern. In no art, he says, do art and nature seem so one as in singing. A perfect voice hides its own art completely.

Part one surveys modern instruction: breathing, registers, resonance. Part two attacks its fallacies one by one, from breath control to nasal resonance and mechanical management of the voice. Part three seeks the basis of a real science of voice. Taylor writes as a reformer with a laboratory mind. The book remains a sharp, readable argument that singing is guided by the ear and mind, not by throat tricks.
22071-marjorie-dean-college-sophomore:
Pauline Lester sent her heroine back to Sanford College in Marjorie Dean, College Sophomore, published in 1922. Marjorie and her friends return for their second year full of plans. Jerry speaks for them all: whose fault is it, she retorts, that she and Muriel have lost last year's trusting faith in reception committees? As freshmen they stood on the station platform like dummies, with no one to bid them the time of day.

The slight rankles, and the Sans Soucians, the campus society at the books' centre, must mend its ways. Lester's Marjorie Dean books followed their heroine through high school and college. This sophomore volume mixes friendship, snobbery, and reform in the series' earnest style.
22211-gilian-the-dreamer-his-fancy-his-l:
Neil Munro, the Scottish novelist of John Splendid, published Gilian the Dreamer in 1899. His subtitle promises Gilian's fancy, his love, and adventure. The book opens by a Highland river as rain beats on plane and beech leaves. The scent of the blossoming gean-tree hangs sweet and haunting round the road.

Gilian is a dreamer in a hard, practical world of Highland trade and kirk. Munro follows his fancies, his love, and his brushes with rougher men. Mist, hills, and old woods colour every chapter, as the opening sigh of wind suggests. The novel is a tender, melancholy piece of the Scottish literary revival.
22218-the-street-that-wasn-t-there:
Clifford D. Simak and Carl Jacobi wrote The Street That Wasn't There for Comet magazine in July 1941. Mr. Jonathon Chambers leaves his house on Maple Street and finds the world subtly wrong. Chambers was once a professor whose book cost him his university post in a scandal. What he taught has been forgotten, but it was revolutionary enough to ruin him.

Now the forgotten theory seems to be coming true around him. Streets, neighbours, and his own past refuse to stay fixed. Simak and Jacobi build the unease quietly, in a small town at evening. The story is a neat early tale of reality slipping, by two masters of the pulp magazines.
22255-the-counts-of-gruye-re:
Mrs. Henry de la Pasture translated The Counts of Gruyère from the French history of the Swiss counts. The book opens on a green plain where the first steps of the Alps rise like an amphitheatre. A little castled city on a solitary hill has watched the scene for a thousand years. That city is Gruyères, and its counts ruled the valley for centuries.

The history follows the counts through crusades, wars, debts, and marriages. The last count, Michael, lost the county in the 1500s, and the castle passed to Fribourg and Bern. De la Pasture, herself a novelist, made the dry records readable. The volume is Swiss local history in its romantic vein.
22280-views-and-reviews-essays-in-apprec:
W. E. Henley, poet and editor, gathered his criticism in Views and Reviews: Essays in Appreciation in 1890. Henley was a formidable judge with a wooden leg and a thunderous taste. On Dickens he is deliciously severe by proxy: Andrew Lang, he notes, mocks those who cannot read Dickens, yet loves only the humourist. For Dickens the artist in drama and romance Lang has as little sympathy as the most practical reader.

Henley himself reads generously and judges sharply. Essays on novelists, poets, and dramatists fill the volume. His criticism is personal, quotable, and often unjust in an interesting way. The book is a monument of the 1890s literary battlefield, where reputations were made by fighting.
22281-the-facts-about-shakespeare:
William Allan Neilson of Harvard and Ashley Horace Thorndike of Columbia wrote The Facts about Shakespeare as a plain handbook. They begin with an England in motion. When Elizabeth came to the throne, England was still largely Catholic after nine centuries. When Shakespeare died, it was Protestant and turning Puritan, and religion, politics, literature, and commerce had all changed around him.

Against that moving background the professors set the documents: baptism, marriage, will, and the Stratford monument. They separate record from legend with scholarly care. The book was written for students who wanted the evidence without the fog. It remains a sober, useful life in brief, all facts and no Bardolatry.
22303-personality-in-literature:
Personality in Literature is a critical essay preserved from Project Gutenberg, with no author named in the record. It opens at an exhibition of Post-Impressionist pictures. The writer walks the show with an artist who helped create it.

Forced to speak in questions, the writer faces a canvas that looks formless and ugly to untrained eyes. That awkward scene sets up the larger topic named in the title. The essay asks how the maker's own character shows through in creative work. Readers get period criticism in a personal voice, caught between polite manners and honest doubt about new art.
22318-crocker-s-hole-from-slain-by-the-d:
Crocker's Hole is one of R. D. Blackmore's tales from Slain by the Doones. Where other Doone stories chase outlaws, this one slows down for water. Its quoted passage follows small streams with loving patience.

Tricklets slip through water-grass, make moss, and forget themselves in the ooze. Kettles are filled from the same small flows at cottage doors. One and all, Blackmore writes, they come to the same thing at last: the river. That gentle close shows his gift for West Country landscape. Readers get a quiet nature piece tucked inside a book of rougher tales.
22752-the-pirate-of-panama-a-tale-of-the:
William MacLeod Raine wrote The Pirate of Panama, a 1914 tale of the fight for buried treasure. Raine, a prolific western novelist, here trades the range for the sea roads of Panama, where tales of pirate gold still drew adventurers in the canal years. His subtitle promises the fight, and the book delivers it.

The opening is all weather and nerves: a chill wind swept the city and cut to the marrow. From a hilltop the narrator watches his car sliding down toward him as he clings to the curb, postponing the plunge into the flowing street. Modern streets give way to older, bloodier trails southward. Raine writes clean, fast adventure in his western manner, transplanted to treasure country.
22866-an-ounce-of-cure:
A doctor's warning opens An Ounce of Cure, a short story about health and denial. Fifty-five is a dangerous age, he tells his patient gravely. He asks about a cough, heartburn after dinner, and sleeping propped on pillows. Then comes the sigh. The man has gone ten years without a checkup.

The tale builds its tension from that ordinary neglect. Prevention, the old proverb promises, beats any cure, and the story tests the proverb on a man who would rather not know. Its setting is the modern clinic rather than the sickroom of older fiction. Readers get a compact, pointed piece of mid-century magazine storytelling, with a moral carried by scene and dialogue rather than lecture.
22996-the-rover-boys-on-snowshoe-island-:
Arthur M. Winfield races his Rover Boys across the ice in The Rover Boys on Snowshoe Island, published in 1918. On a Saturday in early winter, Colby Hall's cadets pack the smooth ice of the lake beside their school. Tag, hockey, and snapping the whip fill the hours until Gif Garrison, head of the athletic association, suggests a race.

Snowshoe Island and an old lumberman's treasure box wait beyond the schoolyard fun. Winfield, writing as the Rover Boys' chronicler, delivers the series formula, sport, mystery, and clean rivalry in equal parts. The cadet setting updates Tom, Dick, and Sam's world for a new generation. Millions of boys read these books, and this volume shows the machine working smoothly.
23014-a-soldier-of-the-empire:
Thomas Nelson Page guards a New Orleans quarter in A Soldier of the Empire. Neighbors came to treat the old Sergeant as the Quarter's true keeper of order. He preserved its quiet better than every gendarme ever posted inside its bounds. And thus the children all knew him.

An old soldier of Napoleon, settled in Louisiana, gives Page his figure of honor out of place and time. The empire fell, but its discipline keeps one neighborhood safe. Page tells the tale in his elegiac register, loyal to lost causes and the men who served them. Beneath the sentiment sits a shrewd portrait of authority earned by character. It is among his characteristic short works, compact and carefully warmed.
23044-the-merry-wives-of-windsor-the-wor:
Textual trouble heads The Merry Wives of Windsor in this Cambridge Shakespeare volume. The editors print the play's early text exactly as the 1602 quarto gives it, using Capell's preserved copy. They check that text against the second quarto of 1619 throughout.

That fuss exists because the Merry Wives survives in two very different early texts. The play inside is Shakespeare's sunniest piece of town comedy, Falstaff scheming after two merry wives who out-scheme him at every turn. Laundry baskets, jealous husbands, and a midnight fright at Herne's oak fill the plot. The edition lets readers enjoy the farce and inspect its foundations on the same page, a double pleasure this series made normal.
23141-the-island-treasure:
Captain Snaggs shouts orders in The Island Treasure. Captain Snaggs barks his orders in quick succession, hoarse words ringing fore and aft until the deck fittings seem to jingle. His drawl carries a strong nasal twang, as though half the speaking came through his nose.

A treasure island, a nasal captain, and a crew under full sail give this sea tale its classic furniture. George Manville Fenn, to whom the adventure is credited, stocked dozens of boys' books with just such gear. Storms, charts, and buried wealth turn the pages in order. The Snaggs portrait alone, all voice and authority, shows a practiced hand.
a-drama-on-the-seashore:
Honoré de Balzac places his short tale on the rocky coast of Brittany, in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's translation. The narrator, walking by the sea with a companion, falls into thought about youth and ambition. They meet a poor fisherman whose worn face and silence hide a dreadful story.

The fisherman's tale, told in brief, concerns a father, a son given to crime, and a punishment the father felt God required of him. The sea and the barren shore frame the confession, and the narrator leaves shaken. Balzac packs guilt, faith, and fate into a few pages, and the stark ending has kept the story in print.
a-girl-of-high-adventure:
A Girl of High Adventure is a 1914 girls' novel by L T Meade, one of the most prolific writers of fiction for young people in her day. Its heroine, Margot St Juste, lives under the care of her Uncle John and his wife. The opening pages show the aunt lecturing the girl on gratitude, warning her that without their kindness she would be a miserable little beggar.

Margot answers her uncle's kindness easily, but life in that strict household is harder than the lectures suggest. From this constrained start, Meade builds the adventure promised by the title, in her usual manner for girl readers of the period. The book preserves a lively example of Edwardian girls' fiction and its mix of duty, spirit, and escape.
a-history-of-english-literature:
Robert Huntington Fletcher wrote A History of English Literature as a college manual, and his preface is dated August 1916. He aimed to outline how the literature grew with the nation's life, judge the chief authors fairly, and still leave students time to read the works themselves rather than books about them.

The survey runs by periods, from the Britons and Anglo-Saxons through the Norman-French age and on toward the nineteenth century, which Fletcher treats at greatest length. Chapters mix biography, criticism, and lists of cheap editions a class could actually buy. Questions and assignments at the end turn the volume into a working textbook, not just a shelf reference.
a-journey-in-other-worlds-a-romance-of-t:
John Jacob Astor imagines a voyage to Jupiter and Saturn, in a romance whose contents include a historical sketch of the world in the year 2000, given by Professor Cortlandt. President Bearwarden speaks, plans are laid, and the ship Callisto is built. Book one handles the future earth before the travelers say goodbye.

Book two explores Jupiter: mastodons, strange hunters, a Jovian Niagara, and polar discoveries. Book three reaches Saturn, where the travelers meet spirits and hear sermons on the soul's fate. Astor, one of America's richest men, mixes science guesses, hunting scenes, and theology. The novel is a curious window into what the future looked like from his decade.
a-study-in-tinguian-folk-lore:
Fay-Cooper Cole submitted this study for his doctorate at Columbia University, publishing it at Chicago in 1915, as the title page states. It rests on a collection of Philippine folk tales he gathered during sixteen months with the Tinguian, a pagan people of the mountain districts of Abra and northern Luzon. He notes their social organization and ceremonies differ sharply from the neighboring Igorot.

Cole analyzes the tales by motif and type, comparing Tinguian stories with those of other peoples to trace how folklore travels and changes. The study is technical, written for fellow anthropologists, but its subject is living story: creation, spirits, and heroes. It stands as an early, serious piece of Philippine folklore scholarship.
adventure:
Jack London's novel was taken from the 1911 Thomas Nelson edition named on its opening page. It begins with a very sick white man carried on the back of a servant in the Solomon Islands. The sick man runs a plantation, and fever has nearly finished him. A ship's arrival brings Joan Lackland, a young woman who wants to become a planter herself.

Twenty-eight chapters follow storms, labour troubles, rival traders, and the hard bargain of island planting. Joan shoots, rides, and argues as an equal, and feeling grows between her and the recovering planter. London fills the tale with trade goods, copra, disease, and the rough rules of the South Seas.
alice-sit-by-the-fire:
J. M. Barrie begins, in his stage directions, by wishing he could peep into Amy's diary. It is octavo, with Amy in gold letters across its soft brown leather covers. It lies padlocked in the lower drawer of a hand-painted escritoire. Amy is sixteen, and today she is washing her hair. Her parents are coming home from India after years away, and she has built a romance around the mother she barely knows.

Alice, the mother, finds grown children who treat her as a stranger and a daughter bent on a tragic love affair copied from novels. Barrie turns the tangle with tenderness: scenes of misunderstanding mend into recognition. The play shows the Peter Pan author writing family feeling without magic, and finding it harder.
along-the-shore:
Rose Hawthorne Lathrop gathers her poems under a shore title, dedicating the volume to G. P. L. The contents open with Inlet and Shore and run through Impersonality, A Protean Glimpse, Life's Priestess, The Shell and the Word, The Clock-Tower Bell, Broken Waves, and The Ghosts of Revellers. Sea pieces stand beside studies of grief, faith, and endurance.

Later titles — The Suicide, For Others, A Song Before Grief, The Baby, Twenty Bold Mariners, In the Artillery, The Lost Battle — show the range from lyric to narrative. Lathrop, Nathaniel Hawthorne's daughter, wrote verse of real feeling before she gave her later life to nursing the poor with cancer. The poems keep her early, literary self in view.
at-aboukir-and-acre: At Aboukir and Acre, G, a, henty's napoleonic tale, the egyptian campaign. This book preserves that historical novel. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
at-the-earth-s-core:
Edgar Rice Burroughs opens At the Earth's Core with a narrator who warns that nobody will believe his story. He tells how David Innes and inventor Abner Perry bored into the earth in a great iron mole. They emerge in Pellucidar, a hollow world lit by a central sun, where time barely moves. Dinosaurs, beast-men, and the reptilian Mahars rule there.

Enslaved, Innes meets Dian the Beautiful, escapes, and fights the Mahars, who paralyze victims in their temple before eating them. The contents promise slavery, freedom, pursuit, and a return to earth. Published in 1914, the novel launched Burroughs's Pellucidar series and mixes lost-world adventure with his usual swift, cliff-hanging pace.
beautiful-stories-from-shakespeare:
E Nesbit retold twenty of Shakespeare's plays as Beautiful Stories from Shakespeare, opening with Dr Johnson's praise that Shakespeare alone gave his country more practical wisdom than all his successors. Her preface calls his works the richest and fairest uninspired genius ever penned, instruction delivered through delight. A brief life of Shakespeare precedes the tales.

A Midsummer Night's Dream, The Tempest, As You Like It, King Lear, and Romeo and Juliet lead the contents, each play compressed into clear prose for young readers. Macbeth demanding which of them has placed Banquo's ghost in his chair shows her fidelity to the drama. Nesbit's versions, like Lamb's Tales before them, started generations toward the plays themselves.
black-bartlemy-s-treasure: Black Bartlemy's Treasure, Jeffery Farnol's pirate adventure. The treasure hunt unfolds. This book preserves that tale. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
brandes-main-currents-in-19th-century-li:
Georg Brandes opens his landmark survey of European writing with The Emigrant Literature, here in English. Exiles driven out by revolt carried new ideas from land to land after the French Revolution. The Danish critic treats their books as sparks in a broad fire.

Brandes links life, politics, and art in one flowing account. He asks how writers in exile shaped the taste of a whole continent. Later volumes would take up France, Germany, and England in turn. This first book launched a six-volume work that changed how Europe read its own nineteenth century.
british-airships-past-present-and-future:
George Whale, a late major in the Royal Air Force, surveyed British Airships from the earliest experiments through the machines of the First World War. Chapters divide the subject among private builders, army airships, and the naval airship section. Named types include Parseval and Astra-Torres ships, the coastal and C Star classes, and the great rigids numbered 1, 9, 23, and 33.

Whale gives dimensions, lifting arrangements, and frank judgments, as when the North Sea airship suffers for its badly designed propelling machinery. Written just after the war, the book also looks forward to airships' commercial future. It preserves technical detail and service gossip that official reports left out.
castle-nowhere:
Castle Nowhere, by Constance Fenimore Woolson, opens on the empty northern curve of Lake Michigan. Woolson describes a shore the school maps leave blank. A hundred miles of shore west of Point St Ignace counts as nothing, by the map makers' account. Jesuit canoes and modern propellers alike cut across and leave it alone. The railroad of the future, she notes dryly, will make British America a garden of roses someday.

Woolson sets her stories in that bypassed wilderness. A castle nowhere is a dwelling built on no route to anywhere. Isolation is her subject and her method. The Great Lakes stories collected here grew from her years on Mackinac Island. She was James Fenimore Cooper's grandniece, and Henry James's friend and rival. Her north is colder than his Europe and as carefully observed. Readers who find the map blank, she promises, are exactly the readers she wants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acre:
Acre, called Saint-Jean-d'Acre, is a Syrian Mediterranean seaport, on a plain with Mount Carmel to the south and the mountains of Galilee to the east. Though choked with sand, it ranks among the best harbours on the Syrian coast. Chanaanite-built and given to Aser's tribe, it was never conquered by them. It passed through Assyrian, Tyrian, Seleucid, and Roman hands, and Claudius granted it municipal rights as Colonia Claudii Caesaris.

Its early Christian community hosted St. Paul. The city was taken by Moslems in 638, by Crusaders in 1104, by Moslems again in 1187, by Crusaders again in 1191, and finally by Moslems in 1291. Napoleon failed before it in 1799, Egypt's viceroy took it in 1832, and the sultan retook it in 1840. Until about 1400 it held a Latin bishop, and it now has a Melchite bishop under Antioch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-in-early:
Adam matters greatly to the Fathers and to apocryphal writers of the first five Christian centuries, as their frequent allusions show. Yet his place in the liturgy is far from prominent. The calendar and one Eastern church hymn carry his name, and he fares little better in the West. The sections referring to him are Holy Saturday's first prophecy and the Genesis readings at Septuagesima time.

In literature, by contrast, Adam is treated generously and becomes hero of several books. They include the Book of the Penance or Combat of Adam and the Struggle of Adam and Eve after the Garden. They also include the Codex Nazaraeus, the Testament of Adam, the Apocalypse of Adam, and the Book of the Daughters of Adam. The Testament survives in fragments of great interest, and the entry follows these works through liturgy and legend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aedh-of-kilda:
Aedh of Kildare, Leinster's king and an Irish saint, is commemorated by Colgan under 4 January, though much obscurity attaches to his life and work. The Four Masters' Annals and Ulster's agree on this monarch, who gave up his crown and eventually became Kildare's bishop. Under Aidus, Aedh's latinized form, his name appears in several martyrologies.

Colgan says he resigned Leinster's throne in 591, really 592, entering Kildare's great monastery for forty-eight years' service to God, rising successively to abbot and bishop. His episcopate ran from about 630 to 639, and he died in 639 by the corrected Ulster chronology. He must not be confused with Aedh Finn, king of Ossory, called Aedh the cleric, a contemporary who also resigned a throne for a monastic cell. Aedh of Leinster was called Aedh Dubh for his dark features, while Ossory's Aedh was fair.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aire:
Aire, also Abram, covers the Landes department's territory. Auch's suffragan under the old regime, re-establishment waited until 1822, when it again became the re-established Auch archdiocese's suffragan. The former Dioceses of Aire and Acqs, or Dax, supplied its territory; history's first mentioned bishop, Marcellus, sat at the Council of Agde in 506.

Among its sixteenth-century bishops was Francois de Foix, Count of Candale, a mathematician who translated Euclid and founded a Bordeaux mathematics chair. Mas d'Aire's Gallo-Roman crypt holds a sarcophagus preserving St. Quitteria's body, martyred perhaps under Commodus for resolving to remain a virgin. Saint-Sever owes its origin to a tenth-century Benedictine abbey built by a Gascon duke in thanks for victory over the Northmen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexandre-guy:
Alexandre Guy Pingré was a French astronomer, born at Paris in September 1711 and dead in May 1796. Educated at Senlis by the Genovefan fathers, he joined their order at sixteen and became professor of theology there in 1735. About 1749 he took the astronomy chair at the new academy of Rouen. He was famous for catching a four-minute error in Lacaille's reckoning of the lunar eclipse of December 1749. In 1753 he observed the transit of Mercury.

Pingré built an observatory at the Abbey of Ste-Geneviève and worked there for forty years, compiling the nautical almanac for 1754. He joined an expedition to Rodriguez to watch the transit of Venus in June 1761, which failed, and saw the transit from Haiti in June 1769. His Cométographie of 1783 to 1784 sifted the history of comets from ancient annals and recent works. The entry defends him against the charge that Jansenist quarrels drove him into provincial posts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alpha-and-ome:
Alpha and Omega, the Greek alphabet's first and last letters, symbolize orthodox confidence in the scriptural proofs of Our Lord's divinity from the fourth century. The Apocalypse suggested the symbol: Christ shares with the Father the titles First and Last. He is the Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. Clement of Alexandria also calls the Word Alpha and Omega.

In early monuments the symbol was most used. The earliest dated occurrence, a Roman inscription of 295, has Omega taking precedence, both letters part of the inscription. Whether the symbol in regular form predates Nicaea in 325 is unsettled; if so, rare. A mid-fourth-century fresco in the Praetextatus catacomb joins Alpha and Omega to the monogrammatic cross. The oldest inscription in traditional form dates from 364. From then on the letters were a favourite orthodox symbol, disfavoured by Arians, found across early Christendom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altars-in-scr:
The English word altar, from alta ara, describes its purpose less well than Hebrew mizbeah, from zabhah, to sacrifice, and Greek thysiasterion, from thyo, to immolate. In the Old Testament the brazen altar stood in the Temple court east of the Temple proper. Twenty cubits long, twenty broad, and ten high, it was larger than the tabernacle altar it resembled. The altar of incense served offerings the entry treats apart, where modern critics diverge from the common opinion.

In the New Testament the word covers the altar of holocaust or of incense. St. Paul argues from the ministers' share in the sacrifice that Gospel ministers should live by the Gospel. Modern critics affirm several legitimate pre-Josian places of worship, a claim the entry notes but does not examine, since only altar regulations concern it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambroise-pare:
Ambroise Paré, French surgeon born at Bourg-Hersent near Laval in 1517, died 20 December 1590. Apprenticed to a barber young, he became barber-surgeon at Paris's Hôtel-Dieu and army surgeon under Francis I. From 1545 he studied anatomy under Sylvius, became surgeon to Henry II in 1552, and first surgeon and chamberlain to Charles IX in 1563. A lifelong Catholic, he was not the Huguenot spared at St. Bartholomew's by royal command, as legend claimed.

His motto read, I treated him, but God healed him. His pioneer military surgery reformed gunshot wound treatment and revived arterial ligation after amputation, against the cauterizing of supposedly poisoned wounds with hot iron or oil. His standing beside Vesalius in anatomy marks his place in modern surgery's rise, and soldiers held him in special regard for his humanity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ampere:
Andre-Marie Ampere, born at Lyons in 1775 and dead at Marseilles in 1836, stands among the founders of the science of electricity and magnetism. As a child he showed a prodigious gift for mathematics. He taught himself Latin to read Bernoulli and Euler, and he was shaken deeply when his father was executed at Lyons during the Revolution in 1793.

After Oersted showed that a current deflects a magnetic needle, Ampere showed within a week that parallel wires carrying currents attract or repel each other. That work laid the ground for electrodynamics, and he published his mathematical theory of the subject in 1830. He also proposed an electric telegraph in 1821. He taught and served as Inspector-General of the University, and he closed his life with a wide philosophical survey of human knowledge, published after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-lefeb:
Antoine Lefebvre, Sieur de la Barre, a French colonial governor born in Paris in 1622, served France in Guiana and Canada. A judge and intendant at home, he sailed in 1664 to settle Guiana, publishing an account of the colony on his return. He later commanded in the Antilles before becoming governor-general of Canada in 1682.

In Canada he followed royal orders to curb the Iroquois and protect French trade, but his expedition to Fort Frontenac failed. Louis the Fourteenth recalled him in 1685, and he later governed Cayenne again until his death in 1690. The entry follows an able administrator whose Canadian command ended in recall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arthur-moore:
Arthur Moore, count, was born at Liverpool in 1849 and died at Mooresfort, Tipperary, in 1904, son of Charles Moore, member of parliament for Tipperary. Educated at Ushaw, he travelled in Spain, and in 1874 won election as member for Clonmel borough. In parliament he followed Butt and strongly backed land reform, better treatment of workhouse children, university access for Irish Catholics, and Home Rule. He took special interest in Catholic chaplains for the fleet.

In 1877 he married a daughter of the English baronet Sir Charles Clifford and received the title of count from the pontiff. During Gladstone's parliament of 1880 to 1885 he usually sided with Parnell, favouring land purchase as the best solution of the Irish question. He urged cottages for Irish labourers and fairer treatment of Irish emigrants aboard ship. He steadily voted for Home Rule and fiercely denounced coercion, while rejecting violent agitation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aubrey-thomas:
Aubrey Thomas Hunt de Vere was an Irish poet, critic, and essayist. He was born at Curragh Chase in County Limerick in 1814 and died there in 1902. A friend of the astronomer William Rowan Hamilton, he came through him to revere Wordsworth and Coleridge. He studied metaphysics at Trinity College Dublin, and later fell under Newman's influence. Days spent under Wordsworth's roof stayed with him as the greatest honor of his life, and he made a pilgrimage to the poet's grave while age allowed.

Study of Coleridge first moved him toward Catholicism, and he was received into the Church at Avignon in 1857, without losing his many friends. He sat as Member of Parliament for Limerick from 1854 to 1859, and his later years at Curragh Chase produced translations from Horace. The entry also records the Gothic church he built there, his slight frame, and a life unmarried to the age of ninety.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baltimore:
Baltimore is the senior see of the United States, founded as a diocese in 1789 and raised to an archdiocese in 1808. It covers Maryland west of Chesapeake Bay plus the District of Columbia, 6,502 square miles in all. Of about 1,273,000 people there, 255,000 were Catholics, chiefly of English, Irish, and German descent. Polish, Lithuanian, Bohemian, and Italian congregations also flourished, with six churches for black Catholics.

Catholic Maryland was planned by George Calvert, founded by his son Cecilius, and named for Queen Henrietta Maria. Its assembly passed the famous religious toleration act in 1649, after Catholic rule since the 1634 landing. Puritans later seized the government and curbed Catholic worship, though liberty later returned. Growth came by natural increase, immigration, and conversion, aided by Cardinal Gibbons and his book The Faith of Our Fathers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-belluno-feltr:
Belluno-Feltre is a diocesan entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, covering two joined sees in Venetia, in northern Italy. Belluno sits on a hill between the Ardo torrent and the Piave river, and its bishops once held temporal rule as counts under an imperial grant of 959. Disputes over the town ran for centuries until its people accepted Venice in 1420.

Feltre shares the later story, and the entry lists bishops, churches, and religious houses across both towns. Statistics on parishes, clergy, and schools close the picture of a mountain diocese with deep medieval roots. The piece is a compact local history built around its bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-andre: Bernard André, an Augustinian friar from Toulouse, was poet laureate of England and chronicler of Henry VII, whose reign ran from 1485 to 1509. Tutor to Prince Arthur and probably to the young Henry VIII, and blind in later life, he wrote mostly in Latin under Renaissance influence. His history of Henry VII remains a rare contemporary source for the Cornish revolt of 1497.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethlehem-in-: Bethlehem, in architecture, is a term used in the Ethiopian Church for the oven or bakehouse where the Korban, or Eucharistic bread, is baked. Coptic churches usually include one as an attachment, generally set within the church enclosure. The entry illustrates it from the plan of Mari Mina and from the monastery of Dair Abu Makar, where the oven stands among monks' cells and domestic buildings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-bernardine:
Blessed Bernardine of Feltre, a Franciscan missionary, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Feltre in 1439, eldest of nine children of the noble Tomitano family, he died at Pavia in 1494. A Lenten course preached by St. James of the Marches at Padua in 1456 moved him to take the Franciscan habit that May.

Studies at Mantua and ordination in 1463 led to a long apostolate, after a miraculous cure of a speech impediment freed his tongue. Counted among the fifteenth century's great Franciscan missionaries, he preached across Italy and founded monti di pietà, pawnshops lending to the poor without usury. The entry presents a preacher and a friend of the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-humphrey-m:
Blessed Humphrey Middlemore, an English Carthusian martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Son of Thomas Middlemore of Edgbaston, an old Warwickshire family, he was professed at the London Charterhouse, ordained, and made procurator, or steward, of the house. Prior John Houghton prized his learning and piety.

Refusal of Henry VIII's oath of supremacy brought the Charterhouse fathers to Tyburn in 1535. Middlemore died there on 19 June, hanged, drawn, and quartered with his prior and a fellow monk. The entry presents a quiet steward among the first Carthusian martyrs of the English Reformation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-byzantine-arc:
Byzantine building blends Greek and Roman forms with Eastern ones, though early on the two strains cannot be cleanly split. The western church plan, a nave on columns with an atrium, appears in fifth-century examples at Byzantium and Rome. The sixth century carried such churches to Ravenna, Istria, and Africa. Vaulted basilicas arose in Asia Minor, Syria, Africa, and Constantinople. The domed style, with barrel-vaulted aisles and transepts, won favor in the East.

That domed type leads to plans built round a center: circular, octagonal, or cross-shaped. The East favored the shape, yet Italy knew it from the fourth and fifth centuries. The apse, the narrow narthex, the eastward facing, and the sharp-cut acanthus leaf cannot be pinned to the East alone. Ravenna's churches, Saint Apollinare and Saint Vitale among them, are too quickly labeled Byzantine. Like features appear in the West as well.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-byzantine-lit:
Byzantine literature voices the mind of the Greek people of the Eastern Roman Empire in the Christian Middle Ages. It blends Greek, Christian, Roman, and Eastern strains on a Roman political base. Greek culture centers not on Athens but on Alexandria, where learned scholarship and popular Jewish-Greek life stood side by side. That split runs through the whole literature, setting a scholarly, rational strain against a romantic, popular one.

The scholarly strain, backed by the Atticizing movement that looked back to classical Athens, held the upper hand until the fall of the empire. Historians and chroniclers, encyclopedists and essayists, secular verse, church and theological writing, and popular poetry all find their place in it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-camille-lefeb:
Camille Lefebvre, apostle of the Acadians, was born at Saint Philippe, Quebec, in 1831 and died at Saint Joseph, New Brunswick, in 1895. Son of sturdy French-Canadian farmers, he taught school, studied Latin, and entered the Congregation of Holy Cross in 1852, becoming a priest in 1855. His gifts as a preacher carried him through curacies, teaching, and missions until 1864, when he took charge of Memramcook and founded Saint Joseph's College.

Since the expulsion of 1755, Acadians in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island had lived without means of schooling or advancement. They were looked down on as hewers of wood and drawers of water. In three decades Lefebvre's college changed that. His students rose in business, the professions, the bar, the legislatures, the federal parliament, and the Supreme Court bench, turning servitude into equality and freedom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonesses-re:
The Canonesses Regular of the Holy Sepulchre trace their foundation only by tradition to Saint James the Apostle, with Saint Helena said to have taken the habit from Saint Macanus of Jerusalem. The first date on record is 1276, when the Saragossa convent was founded. A house at Charleville in 1622, founded by Claudia Mouy, the Marquis de Chaligny's widow, opened a great revival in the West.

A Jesuit Father drew up constitutions, approved by Urban VIII in 1631, binding the canonesses to the Divine Office, strict fasts, the discipline, and a strict reading of poverty. Twelve professed religious were needed to elect a prioress. Susan Hawley founded the English canonesses, leading a community at Liège from 1652. After the Revolution the sisters reached England in 1794, settling at New Hall near Chelmsford, where they still run a boarding school for young ladies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-inv:
Canonical investiture names the act and the rites by which a lord once granted a fief to a vassal. From the middle of the eleventh century the word also covered the way princes gave bishops and abbots their titles. With the titles came the lands and public rights tied to their offices. The entry traces how that usage grew out of the wider feudal ceremony.

Church law books later used the word for the grant of a church office itself. Only from the thirteenth century did it settle into its modern sense, the act of putting a holder in possession of a benefice. That sense matches what canonists call corporal institution. The entry points readers to the related entries on institution and installation for the fuller picture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-casanare:
Casanare is a vicariate apostolic in Colombia, run by Augustinians under the Congregation of Extraordinary Ecclesiastical Affairs. Its city on the river of the same name once belonged to the Diocese of Tunja. Created in 1893 after efforts from 1884, it forms a great triangle bounded by the Meta River, Venezuela, and the Andes. Bogotá, Tunja, and Pamplona are its neighboring dioceses.

In 1893 some 110,000 people were served by only ten priests, and the seat stands at Tamara among towns such as Nunchia, Tame, and Arauca. Jesuit pioneers had built 126 reductions and large, well-furnished churches, but their expulsion in 1767 wrecked the missions, and merchants still display candlesticks from the abandoned churches. By 1907 about thirty missionaries and three Sisters of Charity convents worked there, despite revolutions in 1895 and 1899.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-peri:
Catholic periodical literature began with the printed broadsides of the late fifteenth century. The earliest surviving sheets came from Germany. Florence's Notizie scritte, nicknamed Gazetta for the coin paid to read them, ranked among the first Italian periodicals. From the start these rudimentary sheets carried religious news, and the Jesuit Relations soon showed how early church authorities grasped the new medium.

The article traces this literature country by country across the western world, covering dailies, weeklies, monthlies, quarterlies, and annuals, not only political newspapers but every periodical form. It gives the history of Catholic journalism in each prominent country. It also gives an account of its standing in its own day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-honor:
Charles-Honore Laverdière was a French-Canadian historian born at Chateau-Richer in 1826 and dead at Quebec in 1873. Ordained in 1851, he joined the Quebec Seminary, where he had studied classics and theology, and stayed there until his death. He taught belles-lettres, physics, chemistry, mathematics, music, and drawing. Though his own writings were few, a school history of Canada and some pamphlets, he supervised the re-editing of works that are the very sources of Canadian history.

Chief among them were the Relations des Jésuites of 1858, and the Journal des Jésuites of 1871. Finally came his dearest wish, the Oeuvres de Champlain, for which he wrote the introduction. When the newly completed edition burned entirely, he calmly noted that misprints escaping his vigilance might be avoided next time. His mastery of plain-song also let him publish liturgical works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-choir-in-arch:
An entry on the choir in church architecture, a term full of ambiguity. Strictly, the choir is the part of the church holding the clergy stalls, though the word is loosely used for the whole eastern arm. At Westminster Abbey the stalls stand in the east nave, so no part of the choir lies in the eastern arm. At Canterbury it fills the western bays of the eastern arm.

Early churches such as Santa Maria Maggiore had only nave and sanctuary, with no choir between. The choir grew as the east part of the nave, fenced by low marble walls called cancelli, the source of the word chancel. Isidore of Seville and Honorius of Autun traced choir to the corona, the circle of clergy or singers around the altar. The enclosed central choir, with pulpits for reading Gospel and Epistle, was the last great change of plan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cincture:
An entry on the cincture, or girdle, an article of liturgical dress recognised as such since the ninth century. Now as then it binds the loose, flowing alb so it does not hinder the wearer. Its liturgical character shows in the prayers said while putting it on and in its symbolism of spiritual watchfulness. The Stowe Missal lists it among Mass vestments, perhaps reflecting seventh-century Celtic practice.

Celtic practice, like Greek practice today, had bishops and priests alone wear the girdle, leaving the deacon's tunic ungirded. Early survivals show narrow bands of silk and rich stuff, often embroidered. Modern girdles are preferably flax or hemp, though wool and silk are allowed. The vesting prayer, gird me, O Lord, with purity, marks it as a sign of priestly chastity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-estien:
Claude Estiennot de la Serre, a Benedictine of Saint-Maur born at Varennes in 1639 and dead at Rome in 1699, joined the Benedictines at Vendome and professed there in 1658. After teaching humanities briefly at Pontlevoy, he was sent to Saint-Germain-des-Pres in Paris, where Dom Mabillon recognised his research talent. The two became intimate friends and fellow-workers, walking through Flanders to visit its chief monastic libraries.

In 1670 Estiennot became sub-prior of Saint-Martin's at Pontoise, whose three-volume history was his first published work. His chief work, the Benedictine Antiquities, was compiled between 1673 and 1682, treating France's monastic traditions diocese by diocese. In 1684 he became procurator of his congregation at the Roman Curia and lived in Rome thereafter. En route he gathered material for Mabillon, feeding the Benedictine Annals and the Gallia Christiana, and he collected sixteen volumes of historical fragments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coimbatore:
Leo Kelly's entry covers Coimbatore, a city in Madras in British India. It stands on the River Noyel. In 1901 it held 53,080 people, of whom 3,000 were Catholics. The diocese takes in the Coimbatore district except one taluk. It also takes in the Nilgiris, parts of Malabar country, and the Nelliampathy Hills. Split from the Vicariate Apostolic of Pondicherry in 1846, it became a vicariate in 1850. It became a full diocese on 1 September 1886 under Bishop Joseph Louis Bardon.

Across a population of two and a half million, the diocese counted 37,080 Catholics. They were served by 41 European and 13 native priests, with 14 students in its seminary. Its schools ran from a second-grade college and a high school down to 67 elementary schools with 4,239 pupils. It also kept two hospitals, four orphanages, and an industrial school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-college-of-sa:
Stephen Donovan's entry covers the College of Saint Bonaventure at Quaracchi, near Florence. It stands famous as the literary center of the Order of Friars Minor. Mgr. Bernardino del Vago, Archbishop of Sardis and then minister general, founded it on 14 July 1879. Its first director, Father Fidelis of Fauna, launched the new edition of Saint Bonaventure's works. After his death in 1881, Ignatius Jeiler of Saxony took charge, and Leonard Lemmens followed him in 1902.

Under the Patres editores, the college won a name for critical scholarship. Foremost stands the Opera Omnia of Saint Bonaventure. Beside it run the Analecta Franciscana, four volumes of early order chronicles from 1885 to 1907. Two Bibliotheca series followed, plus the monthly Acta Ordinis and the Archivum Franciscano-Historicum. In 1903 the friars also began a new critical edition of Alexander of Hales.

John Hanrahan's entry follows the College of Saint Isidore in Rome. It was first founded for Spanish Franciscans under Gregory XV. In 1625 the buildings passed to Father Luke Wadding. With sanction from the General of the Friars Minor and the pope, he turned them into a college for Irish Franciscan students. Within a few years over thirty religious lived within its walls. Some years later the number had grown to fifty. Wadding drew able Irish professors, among them Hickey and Fleming.

The college flourished as a home of Irish learning in Rome. Its fortunes broke when French troops occupied Rome in 1798. The community scattered, and its precious manuscripts were moved for safety. They now rest in the order's convent at Merchant's Quay, Dublin. The entry thus joins a house of study to the wider story of Irish scholars in exile.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-comte-de-mais:
Georges Bertrin's entry follows Joseph de Maistre, a French philosophical writer born at Chambéry in Savoy in 1753 and dead at Turin on 26 February 1821. His family, French in origin, had settled in Savoy a century earlier, his father presiding over the Senate. Eldest of ten, Joseph learned from Jesuits, who with his parents gave him love of religion and detestation of eighteenth-century rationalism, which he always opposed. He entered the magistracy in 1774, became assistant fiscal advocate general in 1780, and senator in 1788.

Fleeing the invading French, he served his Sardinian king on mission at Lausanne for four years. His writings, all in French, then Piedmont's literary tongue, include the 1809 Essai sur le principe générateur des constitutions politiques and the Gallican Church treatise of 1821. Bertrin praises ideas bold and penetrating, at times seemingly prophetic, in a French style among the language's ornaments. His younger brother Xavier wrote too.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coptic-litera:

elsie-dinsmore:
Elsie Dinsmore, by Martha Finley, opens in the schoolroom at Roselands, a pleasant room in the old wing of the house. Finley seats the governess Miss Day with her six pupils. Enna, the youngest, is the spoiled darling of both parents. Her lesson is a trial to teacher and scholar alike. Elsie watches from her desk, the gentle counterweight the first chapter sets in place.

Elsie is eight, motherless, and already famous among readers for her piety. Her trials come from a strict father and a household that misunderstands her conscience. Finley's novel, the first of a long series, defined the Sunday school heroine in America. Elsie weeps, prays, forgives, and converts by example. Critics mocked the books for a century. Girls read them anyway, in the millions. Roselands' schoolroom, with its white muslin and rosewood desks, is where that readership was born.
essays-on-work-and-culture:
Essays on Work and Culture, by Hamilton Wright Mabie, asks what labor does to the laborer. Mabie's contents open with the question Tool or Man, then The Man in the Work and Work as Self-Expression. A dedication verse to Henry Van Dyke makes a confession. Our dearest thoughts travel out of reach along the slender wires of speech. That suits a book about the inner life of ordinary jobs.

Later essays take up the pain of youth and the year of wandering. Fellowship, work and pessimism, special training against general training, and concentration each get a chapter, closing with the ultimate aim. Mabie writes against the idea of work as mere wages. A trade rightly seen is self expression. A school is a workshop of character. Culture is what a man brings home from his bench besides his pay.
fashions-in-literature:
Charles Dudley Warner's literary essays are gathered here under the title of the best of them, and the volume opens with a long memorial introduction. The introducer recalls Warner as the most undogmatic of idealists, a writer who used the essay as Addison used it, for serious things handled with gayety. Thirty years of reputation, from My Summer in a Garden onward, stand behind the pieces.

The title essay treats literary taste as fashion, subject to seasons like bonnets. Warner asks why schools of writing rise, reign, and become ridiculous, and what in a book lets it outlive its mode. The companion essays apply the same lens to authors, reputations, and the reading public. It is criticism without dogma, from a man the introduction calls the most companionable of teachers.
five-thousand-miles-underground-or-the-m:
Roy Rockwood's Five Thousand Miles Underground, copyrighted in 1908, sails the airship Flying Mermaid into the earth. Professor Amos Henderson calls for his assistant Washington in the machine shed as the tale opens. Mark and Jack, the boy heroes of the Great Marvel series, join the new machine. A mysterious hole in the ocean draws them downward.

Whale attacks, a cyclone, and a mutiny delay the descent. Down into the earth they pass, many miles below, into a strange draught and a new land. Giants, a fish that walked, a snake-tree, and a temple of treasure crowd the underground world. Rockwood wrote boys' series fiction at industrial speed, under a house name. This volume is his hollow-earth entry, cheerful, impossible, and brisk. The Flying Mermaid comes home, as the last chapter promises, with wonders duly witnessed.
ginx-s-baby-his-birth-and-other-misfortu:
Edward Jenkins published Ginx's Baby in 1870, a satire on Victorian charity built around one unwanted child of the London poor. Ginx, a laborer with too many children already, tries to give the baby away. The contents divide the joke into what Ginx did with him, and what charity and the churches did with him.

Each denomination and society claims the child, baptizes him, litigates over him, and lets him fall through every crack. Chapters invoke Malthus, magistrates, and the milk of human kindness while the baby grows toward ruin. Jenkins wrote to expose real failures in poor relief, and the book's anger made it a sensation that reformers quoted for years.
glaucus-or-the-wonders-of-the-shore:
Charles Kingsley wrote Glaucus, or The Wonders of the Shore to teach Victorian beginners the pleasures of seashore natural history, first published in 1855 and reprinted for decades. The 1890 edition carries coloured illustrations of sea anemones and other shore creatures. Kingsley addresses the book to a young lady friend and keeps the tone inviting.

He explains dredging, describing the rope lengths, bottles, and patience the work needs, then examines what the dredge brings up under a lens. Tubulipora, anemones, and crabs become wonders rather than specimens. Kingsley, a clergyman-naturalist, saw God's workmanship in every tide pool. His book helped start the aquarium craze and still models how to make science writing warm and exact.

Gregory Klimov, a Soviet officer who defected to the West, wrote The Terror Machine about the Soviet administration in occupied Germany after the Second World War. Klimov had served in that administration himself. Edward Crankshaw, a British Soviet expert, prefaced the English edition.

He describes arrests, deportations, informers, and the daily brutality of the occupation machine from inside its offices. The account is a defector's testimony, written in the early Cold War as warning and as evidence. Its detail is its value: names, offices, and methods, unvarnished. The book stands among the classic defector accounts that shaped the West's picture of the Soviet system.

Appendices take up Katyn, the bombing of civilians, and de-Nazification, pressing the charge that the trials were victors' justice. The booklet is a debated piece of revisionist literature, held complete for researchers of the argument.

hardscrabble-or-the-fall-of-chicago-a-ta:
John Richardson's Hardscrabble; or, The Fall of Chicago opens in April 1812 at a farmhouse on the Chicago River. Four miles from the fort, a backwoods master lingers by his blazing logs. His hunting-frock, fringed homespun, and sheath knife mark him a denizen of the forest. A grizzled voyageur in a beaded sash serves under him.

Richardson builds his tale of Indian warfare toward the Fort Dearborn massacre of August 1812, when Chicago's garrison and settlers were destroyed evacuating the fort. The farm at Hardscrabble becomes the settlers' refuge and strongpoint. Potawatomi warriors, a half-breed villain, and a kidnapped heroine drive the frontier plot. Richardson had served in the War of 1812 himself, and wrote Canada's first novels. His Chicago is no city yet, only a stockade, a river, and farms waiting for the blow he knew was coming.
here-there-and-everywhere:
Here, There and Everywhere, by Lord Frederic Hamilton, is a diplomat's memoir of people and places, published in London in 1921. Hamilton opens in India, at a tiger shoot in Cooch Behar. The Maharajah's howdahs go down in a long line to the covert side. A probable tiger is reported in the grass jungle ahead. The beat stops. Three hundred yards of jungle front must be covered before the guns are posted.

Hamilton served abroad for years and dined everywhere. His chapters move between courts, camps, and country houses with a raconteur's ease. The tiger shoot sets the pattern: ceremony first, then danger, then the anecdote told at dinner. Empire appears in these pages as a social world before it is a system. Its author knew the princes and the proconsuls personally. He writes of both as characters in a club story that happens to span three continents.
history-of-american-literature:
History of American Literature, by Reuben Post Halleck, is a school textbook from the author of a widely used English literature history. Halleck explains in his preface that requests from all parts of the United States produced the book. He studied at first hand, he says, far more than a condensed textbook can hold. Judgment and selection need that background. His chapters describe the greatest achievements in American writing from the earliest times to the present.

Halleck warns against dwelling on minor authors. Half is greater than the whole, he quotes, when the half is the essential. Great authors, literary movements, ideals, and animating principles get the attention. American writing is kept in relation to English literature throughout. The book taught several school generations their national canon. Rip Van Winkle's return illustrates the front matter. Irving, the Knickerbockers, and the Hudson valley open the story Halleck's students learned by heart.
hoadly-queries-recommended-to-the-author: Queries recommended to the authors of the late Discourse of free thinking, by Hoadly. The bishop's queries. This book preserves that pamphlet. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Time has kept the file intact through the years.
how-to-fail-in-literature-a-lecture:
Andrew Lang delivered How to Fail in Literature as a lecture at the South Kensington Museum, for a college for working men and women, and printed it in 1890 much enlarged. Lang asks why people take up writing, what success they should want, and why most of them will fail. His answer is a comedy of vocation: many feel the call, few have the gift, and the smallest class of all has both gift and will.

Advice arrives upside down, as counsel on failing well: mistake ambition for talent, scorn pains, and trust the poetic temperament. Lang, who succeeded at nearly every kind of writing, salts the jokes with real wisdom about style, reading, and work. Aspiring authors still quote it.
indian-why-stories-sparks-from-war-eagle:
Frank Bird Linderman collected Indian Why Stories from Blackfeet elders in Montana, subtitled sparks from War Eagle's lodge-fire. War Eagle tells children why the chipmunk's back is striped, how the ducks got fine feathers, and why the kingfisher wears a war-bonnet. Linderman dedicates the book to artist Charles M Russell and to George Bird Grinnell.

Many tales feature Old-man, the trickster creator, stealing the sun's leggings, outwitting animals, and getting outwitted in turn. Linderman knew his tellers personally and worried that settlement was ending their world. His preface mourns the passing frontier while the stories themselves stay lively, funny, and exact about animal nature as Blackfeet tradition understood it.
kansas-women-in-literature:
Kansas Women in Literature is Nettie Garmer Barker's survey of women writers of Kansas. Its epigraphs boast that the state's children are a nobler pride than its walls of corn. Barker counts Kansas-born and adopted women alike in her galaxy of bright names. The first portrait treats Effie Graham, head of mathematics at Topeka High School.

Graham, Barker says, found romance in arithmetic and showed others the way in her lecture Living Arithmetic. Ex-Governor Hoch called her one of the most gifted women in a state noted for brilliant women. Graham lectured on moving into the king row, other people's children, and the larger service. Barker's sketches mix biography, praise, and quotation. The book preserves a state's pride in its women of letters.
kennedy-square:
Kennedy Square is a novel by F. Hopkinson Smith, set in a Southern square of the late fifties. Smith's preface quotes his own Fortunes of Oliver Horn for the square's portrait: magnolias, glossy box, and Noah's Ark church. Kennedy Square has no church, but it has an archdeacon's house instead. Its atmosphere, he promises, matches the older book's square.

Chapter one opens some sixty years earlier, in the square's great days. Smith builds his story on the square's families, their pride, their money troubles, and their honor. The Civil War era closes around them as the novel proceeds. Smith wrote of old Baltimore society with a painter's eye and a native's affection. Kennedy Square is his tribute to that vanishing world.
king-of-the-khyber-rifles-a-romance-of-a:
King of the Khyber Rifles: A Romance of Adventure is Talbot Mundy's 1916 novel of India's frontier, here in a combined edition. Its contents list eighteen chapters without titles. Captain Athelstan King of the Indian service is the hero. He works among the tribes of the Khyber Pass country, where Britain watched the road to Afghanistan.

The Khyber Rifles, the famous frontier regiment, give the book its name and setting. Mundy's tale mixes secret missions, tribal councils, and mountain fighting. A hidden valley and a mysterious woman stand at the center of the intrigue, by common report of the novel. Mundy knew India well and wrote its frontier with an insider's love of intrigue. The book made his name in adventure fiction.
kitty-trenire:
Mabel Quiller-Couch wrote Kitty Trenire, a story for young readers in twenty-one chapters. The opening chapters bring news, a drive, and storms at home and abroad. Kitty's family and friends fill the early scenes.

Later chapters bring Anna's arrival, lessons, alarms, and an exciting night. One chapter is called Missing, and another is called Banished. A girl named Betty has an escapade of her own. The book closes with a chapter titled Good in Everything, hinting at lessons learned through trouble. Home troubles matter as much as outdoor adventures here. Kitty must carry real duties while she is still quite young.
la-grenadiere:
Honoré de Balzac set his tale La Grenadière in a small house by the Loire. Ellen Marriage translated it into English. The house stands about a mile below the bridge of Tours.

Balzac describes white stone houses among gardens and vineyards along the cliffs. The finest fruit ripens there under a southern exposure. Generations of patient work cut terraces into the rock face. Against that calm, rich setting, he places a quiet story of a woman and her sons. Place matters deeply in this tale of a mother and sons. The calm house frames lives marked by loss and duty.
lady-baltimore:
Owen Wister, author of Western fiction, set his novel Lady Baltimore in the South. He dedicated it to S. Weir Mitchell with lifelong affection. A note to readers opens the book on a playful, serious theme.

Wister quotes Burns on seeing ourselves as others see us. He wishes artists could test their work as its audience first. That wish frames a story of manners and memory in an old Southern city. A young visitor meets a proud, fading society there. Romance and gentle comedy carry the clash of old and new ways.
lady-clare:
